title: Optimising latency and cost in production pipelines

videos.script: A prompt that works has two more numbers to answer to. How long a customer waits for it, and what it costs a million times over. {{numbers}} This lesson starts with the clock. A model reads your prompt in one pass, and writes its answer one token at a time. So the answer's length decides the wait far more than the prompt's. {{time}} On a laptop's processor, twice the input added a tenth of a second. The bare prompt's chatty answers tripled the wait. {{bars}} Then the money. Every token has a price, written in whole cents per million, and the program multiplies integers and rounds once, at the end. You will see why a float has no business near a bill. {{cost}} Then you cut. Taking out the examples makes the prompt a third cheaper and a little faster. It also breaks nine messages in forty, and the sign test says that is no accident. {{broken}} By the end you can say what a saving costs in answers, and read latency the way a waiting person feels it, by the slow calls. {{close}}
